drivingQuestion: Does flesh that separates from a living animal impart impurity, and what status does such food have once it has served a purpose other than being eaten?
outcomeNote: Rava's principle — food that served a non-food function served as wood — stands, and is applied without dissent to five rulings that Abaye, Rav Pappa and Rav Mattana had each explained as only rabbinic.

segments.he: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ בָּשָׂר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ (מֵאֵבֶר בְּהֵמָה), דְּאִילּוּ בָּשָׂר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי – לֹא מְטַמֵּא, מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַנְּבֵלָה – מְטַמֵּא.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: The difference «between them» is with regard to «flesh that separates from the limb of an animal, as flesh that separates from a limb» severed «from the living does not impart impurity,» just like flesh that separates directly from a living animal. By contrast, an olive-bulk of flesh that separates «from the limb of a carcass imparts impurity» like the flesh of a carcass.

segments.he: אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי דִּמְטַמֵּא, מַאי קְרָא? אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: ״וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה״.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «What is the verse» from which it is derived «that a limb» severed «from the living imparts impurity? Rav Yehuda says» that «Rav says:» With regard to the impurity of a carcass it is written: «“And if some animal [min habehema]» of which you may eat «dies,» he who touches its carcass shall be impure until evening” (Leviticus 11:39). The phrase “some animal [min habehema],” which also means: From an animal, is interpreted as indicating that a limb torn from an animal is included in the impurity discussed in the verse.

segments.he: וְהַאי מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לִכְאִידַּךְ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּמַתְנִיתָא תָּנָא: ״וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה״ – מִקְצָת בְּהֵמָה מְטַמְּאָה, וּמִקְצָת בְּהֵמָה אֵינָהּ מְטַמְּאָה, וְאֵיזוֹ זוֹ? זוֹ טְרֵפָה שֶׁשְּׁחָטָהּ!
segments.en: The Gemara asks: How can Rav interpret this verse in such a manner? «This» verse «is necessary for» another halakha «that Rav Yehuda» said that «Rav said,» as «Rav Yehuda said» that «Rav said, and some say it was taught in a baraita:» In the verse: «“And if some animal [min habehema]» of which you may eat «dies,» he who touches its carcass shall be impure until evening,” the phrase “some animal [min habehema]” indicates that «some» dead «animals impart impurity» as a carcass, «and some» dead «animals do not impart impurity» as a carcass. «And which is that» animal that does not impart impurity as a carcass? «That is an animal with a wound that will cause it to die within twelve months [tereifa] that one slaughtered.» Even though slaughter does not render the animal permitted to be eaten, it removes the animal from the category of a carcass with regard to impurity.

segments.he: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא ״מִבְּהֵמָה״, מַאי ״מִן הַבְּהֵמָה״? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ תַּרְתֵּי.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: «If so,» if the verse teaches only one of the two halakhot, «let the Merciful One write mibehema,» in one Hebrew word. «What» is the verse teaching when it states: «“Min habehema,”» with two Hebrew words? It is teaching that one should «conclude two» conclusions «from it.»

segments.he: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ בָּשָׂר נָמֵי? לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ, דְּתַנְיָא: יָכוֹל יְהֵא בָּשָׂר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מִן הַחַי טָמֵא? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה״ – מָה מִיתָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ עוֹשָׂה חֲלִיפִין, אַף כֹּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה חֲלִיפִין, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
segments.en: The Gemara challenges: «If so,» if this verse teaches that a limb from a living animal imparts impurity, one can «also» derive from it that «even flesh» from a living animal imparts impurity. The Gemara responds: «It should not enter your mind» to derive this, «as it is taught» in a baraita: One «might» have thought that «flesh that separates from a living» animal «is impure» like a carcass. Therefore, «the verse states: “And if some animal» of which you may eat «dies.” Just as death does not generate a replacement,» i.e., life is not regenerated from the dead, «so too any» element of an animal «that» dies and «does not generate a replacement» assumes the impurity of a carcass. An animal does not replace a severed limb but it does replace severed flesh; this is «the statement of Rabbi Yosei.»

segments.he: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: ״בְּהֵמָה״, מָה בְּהֵמָה – גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת, אַף כֹּל – גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת. רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: ״בְּהֵמָה״ מָה בְּהֵמָה – בָּשָׂר גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת, אַף כֹּל – בָּשָׂר גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת.
segments.en: «Rabbi Akiva says:» One can derive this halakha from the word «“animal”» in the verse. «Just as an animal» contains «sinews and bones, so too, any» element of an animal that contains «sinews and bones» imparts impurity. Therefore, a limb, which contains sinews and bones, imparts impurity, but flesh, which does not contain sinews and bones, does not impart impurity. «Rabbi» Yehuda HaNasi «says:» One can derive this halakha from the word «“animal”» in the verse. «Just as an animal» contains «flesh, sinews, and bones, so too, any» element of an animal that contains «flesh, sinews, and bones» imparts impurity.

segments.he: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רַבִּי לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא? אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ אַרְכוּבָּה.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «What» difference «is there between» the opinions of «Rabbi» Yehuda HaNasi «and Rabbi Akiva?» The Gemara answers: The practical difference «between them is» with regard to the «leg joint,» which contains sinews and bones but no flesh. According to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi it does not impart impurity when it separates from a living animal, but according to Rabbi Akiva it does.

segments.he: בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי, מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ? אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כּוּלְיָא וְנִיב שְׂפָתַיִם אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «What» practical difference «is there between» the opinions of «Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili? Rav Pappa said:» The practical difference «between them is» with regard to the «kidney and» the «upper lip» that separate from a living animal. According to Rabbi Yosei these parts of the animal impart impurity because the animal does not generate a replacement for them; according to Rabbi Akiva they do not impart impurity, because they do not contain bones.

segments.he: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי גַּבֵּי שְׁרָצִים כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא: יָכוֹל בָּשָׂר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מִן הַשְּׁרָצִים יְהֵא טָמֵא? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״בְּמוֹתָם״ – מָה מִיתָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ עוֹשָׂה חֲלִיפִין, אַף כֹּל שֶׁאֵינָהּ עוֹשָׂה חֲלִיפִין. דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי.
segments.en: The Gemara states a different halakha where these three tanna’im express the same opinions. «So too, it is taught» in a baraita «with regard to creeping animals like this case:» One «might» have thought that «flesh that separates from a creeping animal» during its lifetime «should be impure» like a creeping animal carcass. Therefore, «the verse states» with regard to creeping animal carcasses: “And upon whatever any of them falls «when they are dead» shall be impure” (Leviticus 11:32). The word “dead” teaches that «just as death does not generate a replacement, so too any» element of a creeping animal «that» dies and «does not generate a replacement» imparts the impurity of a creeping animal carcass, excluding flesh; this is «the statement of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.»

segments.he: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: ״שֶׁרֶץ״, מָה שֶׁרֶץ – גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת, אַף כֹּל – גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת. רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: ״שֶׁרֶץ״, מָה שֶׁרֶץ – בָּשָׂר גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת, אַף כֹּל – בָּשָׂר גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת.
segments.en: «Rabbi Akiva says:» One can derive this halakha from the term «“creeping animal.” Just as a creeping animal» contains «sinews and bones, so too any» element of a creeping animal that contains «sinews and bones» imparts impurity. «Rabbi» Yehuda HaNasi «says:» One can derive this halakha from the term «“creeping animal.” Just as a creeping animal» contains «flesh, sinews, and bones, so too, any» element of a creeping animal that contains «flesh, sinews, and bones» imparts impurity.

segments.he: בֵּין רַבִּי לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ אַרְכוּבָּה. בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ? אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כּוּלְיָא וְנִיב שְׂפָתַיִם אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.
segments.en: The Gemara comments: The practical difference «between» the opinions of «Rabbi» Yehuda HaNasi «and Rabbi Akiva is» with regard to «the leg joint,» which contains sinews and bones but no flesh. «What» difference «is there between» the opinions of «Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili? Rav Pappa said:» The practical difference «between them is» with regard to «the kidney and the upper lip,» which contain no bones and which are not regenerated by the creeping animal.

segments.he: וּצְרִיכָא, דְּאִי אַשְׁמְעִינַן בְּהֵמָה – הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּלֹא מְטַמֵּא מֵחַיִּים, מִשּׁוּם דְּלֹא מְטַמֵּא בְּכַעֲדָשָׁה, אֲבָל שֶׁרֶץ דִּמְטַמֵּא בְּכַעֲדָשָׁה – אֵימָא לְטַמֵּא מֵחַיִּים.
segments.en: «And it is necessary» to teach this halakha both with regard to flesh that separates from a living animal and with regard to flesh that separates from a creeping animal. «As if» the baraita «had taught us» this halakha only with regard to «an animal,» one might have said that «this is the reason that» flesh that separates «from a living» animal «does not impart impurity:» It is «because» an animal carcass «does not impart impurity in» the measure of «a lentil-bulk,» but rather only in the measure of an olive-bulk. «But» with regard to «a creeping animal, which imparts impurity» even «in» the measure of «a lentil-bulk, say» that flesh that separates «from» it while it is «living should impart impurity.»

segments.he: וְאִי אַשְׁמְועִינַן שֶׁרֶץ, מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא מְטַמֵּא בְּמַשָּׂא – לֹא מְטַמֵּא מֵחַיִּים, אֲבָל בְּהֵמָה, דִּמְטַמֵּא בְּמַשָּׂא – אֵימָא תְּטַמֵּא מֵחַיִּים, צְרִיכָא.
segments.en: «And if» the baraita «had taught us» this halakha only with regard to «a creeping animal,» one might have said that flesh that separates from a creeping animal does not impart impurity «because» a creeping animal «does not impart impurity via carrying,» and therefore flesh that separates from it «while it is living does not impart impurity. But» with regard to «an animal, which imparts impurity via carrying, say» that flesh that separates from it «while it is living should impart impurity.» Therefore, «it is necessary» to teach this halakha in both cases.

segments.he: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַחוֹתֵךְ כְּזַיִת בָּשָׂר מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, חֲתָכוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ חִישֵּׁב עָלָיו – טָהוֹר.
segments.en: §The Gemara continues to discuss flesh that separates from a living animal. «The Sages taught» in a baraita: In the case of «one who severs an olive-bulk of flesh from a limb» severed «from the living,» the flesh does not impart the impurity of a carcass but it does impart impurity as food if one designated it as food before it came into contact with a source of impurity. Therefore, if «one severed» the flesh from the limb «and afterward intended it» to be used for the consumption of a gentile, the flesh remains «pure» because at the time he designated the flesh as food it was not in contact with a source of impurity.

segments.he: חִישֵּׁב עָלָיו, וְאַחַר כָּךְ חֲתָכוֹ – טָמֵא.
segments.en: But if «he intended it» to be used for the consumption of a gentile «and afterward severed» the flesh, the flesh is «impure,» because it came into contact with a source of impurity, i.e., the limb, after it was designated as food.

segments.he: רַבִּי אַסִּי לָא עָל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא, אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ לְרַבִּי זֵירָא, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי אֲמוּר בְּבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא? אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי קַשְׁיָא לָךְ? אֲמַר לֵיהּ, דְּקָתָנֵי: חִישֵּׁב וְאַחַר כָּךְ חֲתָכוֹ טָמֵא.
segments.en: One day «Rabbi Asi did not go to the study hall. He found Rabbi Zeira,» and «said to him: What was said» today «in the study hall?» Rabbi Zeira «said to him: What» matter is «difficult for you» that you think may have been discussed in the study hall? Rabbi Asi «said to him:» I find difficult that «which is taught» in a baraita: If «one intended» flesh from a limb that was severed from a living animal to be used for the consumption of a gentile, «and afterward he severed» the flesh from the limb, the flesh is «impure.»

segments.he: טוּמְאַת בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים הִיא, וְטוּמְאַת בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים לָא מְטַמְּיָא.
segments.en: Why should the flesh be impure? Since the source of its impurity is the limb, and the location of the contact between the limb and the flesh is hidden and not visible, «it» constitutes contact with a source of «impurity» in «a concealed part» of the body, «and» the principle is that contact with a source of «impurity» in «a concealed part» of the body «does not render» an item «impure.»

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַף לְדִידִי קַשְׁיָא לִי, וּשְׁאֵילְתֵּיהּ לְרַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל, וְאָמַר לִי: הָא מַנִּי? רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא, דְּאָמַר: טוּמְאַת בֵּית הַסְּתָרִים מְטַמְּיָא.
segments.en: Rabbi Zeira «said to» Rabbi Asi: This matter is «difficult for me as well, and I asked Rabbi Abba bar Memel, and he said to me:» In accordance with «whose» opinion «is this» baraita? «It is» in accordance with the opinion of «Rabbi Meir, who said» that contact with a source of «impurity» in «a concealed part» of the body «renders» an item «impure.»

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְלָאו זִימְנִין סַגִּיאִין אַמְרַהּ קַמַּאי, וַאֲמַרִי לֵיהּ: שָׁנֵי לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר בֵּין טוּמְאָה דְּבָעֲיָא הֶכְשֵׁר וּבֵין טוּמְאָה דְּלָא בָּעֲיָא הֶכְשֵׁר.
segments.en: Rabbi Asi «said to» Rabbi Zeira: «But hasn’t» Rabbi Abba bar Memel «said» this answer «in my presence many times? And I said to him» that this answer does not explain the ruling of the baraita. The reason is that with regard to a concealed part of the body imparting impurity, «Rabbi Meir differentiates between» a type of «impurity that requires» an item to be «rendered susceptible» in order to take effect «and» a type of «impurity that does not require» an item to be «rendered susceptible.» The case in the baraita is one where the flesh was not yet rendered susceptible to impurity when it was severed from the limb, and Rabbi Meir concedes that in such a case impurity should not apply to a concealed part of the body.

segments.he: אָמַר רָבָא: וּמַאי קוּשְׁיָא? דִּלְמָא בְּשֶׁהוּכְשַׁר.
segments.en: «Rava» was surprised by Rabbi Asi’s statement and «said: But what is the difficulty? Perhaps» the baraita is discussing a case «where» the flesh «was rendered» susceptible to impurity before it was severed from the limb.

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר רַב חָנָן לְרָבָא: לְמָה לִי הֶכְשֵׁר, הֲרֵי מְטַמֵּא טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה אַגַּב אָבִיו?
segments.en: «Rabba bar Rav Ḥanan said to Rava: Why do I» need the flesh severed from the limb to be «rendered susceptible» to impurity? Flesh that is upon a limb from a living animal «imparts a severe» form of «impurity due to its original» limb, as it is considered part of the limb that was severed from a living animal, which imparts the impurity of a carcass, a severe form of impurity that is transmitted even to people and vessels. Therefore, it is not necessary to render this flesh susceptible to impurity after its separation from the limb, because the halakha is that any food item that will eventually impart a severe form of impurity does not require contact with liquid in order to be rendered susceptible to imparting a lesser form of impurity.

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ, מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: Rava «said to» Rabba bar Rav Ḥanan: This principle applies only when the more severe and more lenient forms of impurity are both impurities of food. But in the case of the baraita, the flesh needs to be rendered susceptible to impurity after it is severed from the limb, because «when it» initially «served» as part of the limb, «it performed the role of wood,» i.e., it had the status of flesh of the limb, which is necessary to give the limb the status of a limb severed from the living (see 128b), but it was not impure due to its status as food.

segments.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ כּוֹפֶת שְׂאוֹר שֶׁיִּחֲדָהּ לִישִׁיבָה – בָּטְלָה.
segments.en: §Rava said that if a food item serves a function other than food, the principle that if it will eventually contract a severe form of impurity it does not require contact with liquid in order to be rendered susceptible to a lesser form of impurity does not apply. The Gemara now relates a number of matters that are explained with the same reasoning. «Abaye said:» The Sages «said» in a baraita: «A mass of» hardened «leaven that one designated for» the purpose of «sitting» upon it, not for consumption, «is nullified.» The item is no longer considered food and one may possess it in his house during Passover. But the item is now considered a chair, and it is subject to ritual impurity imparted by treading. It therefore is rendered impure if a zav sits on it.

segments.he: טוּמְאָתָהּ לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, מָצִינוּ לָאֳכָלִין שֶׁמְּטַמְּאִין טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה, כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ – מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: Abaye explained: «Its impurity» in such a case is clearly «not by Torah law» but by rabbinic law; «as if it enters your mind» that it is impure «by Torah law,» then «we have found» that «food can become susceptible to a severe» type of «impurity.» This cannot be true, because the category of food that requires contact with liquid to be susceptible to impurity is food that will not eventually impart a more severe type of impurity. Based on Rava’s reasoning, the Gemara responds: The seat imparts impurity by Torah law. «When» the leaven «served» as a chair it was not considered food, as «it performed the role of wood.»

segments.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ תִּקְרוֹבֶת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁל אֳכָלִין מְטַמְּאִין בְּאוֹהֶל, טוּמְאָתָהּ לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא – מָצִינוּ לָאֳכָלִין שֶׁמְּטַמְּאִין טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה! כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ – מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: Similarly, «Abaye said:» The Sages «said» in a baraita: «An idolatrous offering of food imparts impurity in a tent.» Abaye explained: «Its impurity is not by Torah law» but by rabbinic law; «as if it enters your mind» that it is impure «by Torah law,» then «we have found» that «food can become susceptible to a severe» type of «impurity.» The Gemara responds: The idolatrous offering imparts impurity by Torah law. «When» the food «served» as an idolatrous offering it was not considered food, as «it performed the role of wood.»

segments.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ חִבּוּרֵי אֳכָלִין כְּכֵלִים דָּמוּ, טוּמְאָתָן לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא – מָצִינוּ לְאוֹכֶל שֶׁמְּטַמֵּא טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה! כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ – מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: Similarly, «Abaye said:» The Sages «said» in a baraita: «Foods that are connected» to vessels are considered «like the vessels.» For example, if dough is attached to a kneading bowl and the owner wishes for the dough to remain there, the dough is considered part of the bowl. Therefore, if an olive-bulk of a corpse touches that dough, it becomes impure with the more severe impurity of a vessel, which imparts impurity to people and other vessels. Abaye explained: «Their impurity is not by Torah law» but by rabbinic law; «as if it enters your mind» that it is impure «by Torah law,» then «we have found» that «food can become susceptible to a severe» type of «impurity.» The Gemara responds: Food connected to vessels imparts impurity by Torah law. «When» the food «served» as a connection to the vessel it was not considered food, as «it performed the role of wood.»

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְרָבָא: הָא דְּתַנְיָא, חֵלֶב נְבֵלָה בַּכְּפָרִים צָרִיךְ מַחְשָׁבָה וְהֶכְשֵׁר, טוּמְאָתוֹ אַגַּב כּוּלְיָא לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, מָצִינוּ לְאוֹכֶל שֶׁמְּטַמֵּא טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה!
segments.en: Similarly, «Rav Pappa said to Rava» in explanation of «that which is taught» in a mishna (Okatzin 3:3): «Fat» forbidden in consumption for a Jew from «an animal carcass in the villages, requires designation» as food in order for it to become susceptible to contract impurity as food, «and» it must be «rendered susceptible» via contact with liquid. Rav Pappa explained: Although the forbidden fat that covers the kidney of a carcass imparts the impurity of a carcass, «its impurity due to» the impurity of the «kidney is not by Torah law» but by rabbinic law. «As if it enters your mind» that it is impure «by Torah law,» then «we have found» that «food can impart a severe» type of «impurity» and subsequently become susceptible to impurity as food.

segments.he: כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ – מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: The Gemara responds: The fat of a carcass imparts impurity by Torah law. «When» the fat «served» the kidney as protection and imparted the impurity of a carcass it did not serve as food, as «it performed the role of wood.»

segments.he: אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה: הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ בַּיִת שֶׁסִּכְּכוֹ בִּזְרָעִים – טָהֵרוּ. טוּמְאָתוֹ לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא – מָצִינוּ לִזְרָעִים שֶׁמְּטַמְּאִין טוּמְאָה חֲמוּרָה! כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ – מַעֲשֵׂה עֵץ שִׁימֵּשׁ.
segments.en: Similarly, «Rav Mattana said:» The Sages «said» in a baraita: With regard to «a house that one roofed with seeds,» i.e., vegetation, if those seeds were impure, they are rendered «pure» when they are used as the roof of the house. The seeds are no longer considered food but rather part of the house. Therefore, if the house becomes leprous, the entire house becomes impure. Rav Mattana explained: «Its impurity is not by Torah law» but by rabbinic law; «as if it enters your mind» that it is impure «by Torah law,» then «we have found» that «seeds can become susceptible to a severe» type of «impurity.» The Gemara responds: The seeds used for the roof of the house impart impurity by Torah law. «When» the seeds «served» as the roof of the house they were not considered food, but rather «performed the role of wood.»

moves.cueHe: איכא בינייהו בשר הפורש ממנו
moves.summary: answers a מאי בינייהו posed at the close of the preceding unit: the difference is flesh separating from a limb of a living animal versus from a limb of a carcass
moves.about: what practical difference separates the two views set against each other at the end of the preceding unit — flesh separating from a limb of a living animal versus from a limb of a carcass

moves.cueHe: אבר מן החי דמטמא, מאי קרא?
moves.summary: asks the scriptural source for a limb from a living animal imparting impurity
moves.about: the scriptural source for the rule that a limb severed from a living animal imparts carcass impurity

moves.cueHe: אמר רב יהודה אמר רב
moves.summary: supplies, in Rav's name, the verse ״וכי ימות מן הבהמה״, whose partitive מן includes a severed limb
moves.about: Rav Yehuda reports Rav's derivation of limb-from-the-living impurity from the phrase מן הבהמה

moves.cueHe: והאי מיבעי ליה לכאידך דרב יהודה אמר רב
moves.summary: objects that the verse is already needed for Rav's other derivation, that a slaughtered tereifa does not impart carcass impurity
moves.about: whether this verse can yield limb-from-the-living impurity when it is already required for Rav's other derivation, that a slaughtered tereifa does not impart carcass impurity

moves.cueHe: אם כן, לכתוב רחמנא ״מבהמה״
moves.summary: answers that the two-word ״מן הבהמה״ instead of ״מבהמה״ is surplus enough to yield both derivations
moves.about: answering its own difficulty: the verse's redundant wording supports both derivations at once

moves.cueHe: אי הכי, אפילו בשר נמי?
moves.summary: presses that the same surplus should include flesh separating from a living animal
moves.about: if the surplus wording teaches that a limb from a living animal imparts impurity, flesh separating from a living animal should be included too

moves.cueHe: לא סלקא דעתך, דתניא
moves.summary: answers with a baraita in which R' Yosei HaGelili expounds ימות to limit impurity to what does not regenerate, excluding flesh
moves.about: flesh is excluded, as a baraita expounds the same verse to limit impurity to what does not regenerate

moves.cueHe: רבי עקיבא אומר: ״בהמה״
moves.summary: derives the same exclusion instead from ״בהמה״: only what has sinews and bones imparts impurity
moves.about: what feature of the verse excludes flesh separating from a living animal from carcass impurity — failure to regenerate, or the absence of sinews and bones

moves.cueHe: רבי אומר: ״בהמה״
moves.summary: derives from ״בהמה״ that flesh, sinews and bones together are required
moves.about: whether the word בהמה requires only sinews and bones, or flesh, sinews and bones together, for carcass impurity

moves.cueHe: מאי איכא בין רבי לרבי עקיבא?
moves.summary: asks what practical case divides Rabbi from R' Akiva
moves.about: what practical case separates Rabbi's requirement of flesh, sinews and bones from R' Akiva's requirement of sinews and bones

moves.cueHe: איכא בינייהו ארכובה
moves.summary: the leg joint, which has sinews and bones but no flesh
moves.about: the leg joint, which has sinews and bones but no flesh, is the case that divides them

moves.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי, מאי איכא בינייהו?
moves.summary: asks what practical case divides R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili
moves.about: what practical case separates R' Akiva's sinews-and-bones criterion from R' Yosei HaGelili's non-regeneration criterion

moves.cueHe: אמר רב פפא: כוליא וניב שפתים
moves.summary: the kidney and upper lip, which do not regenerate but contain no bone
moves.about: the kidney and the upper lip, which do not regenerate but have no bone, are the cases that divide R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili

moves.cueHe: תניא נמי גבי שרצים כהאי גוונא
moves.summary: adduces the parallel baraita on creeping animals, where R' Yosei HaGelili expounds ״במותם״ the same way
moves.about: brings the parallel baraita in which the same three tannaim dispute over flesh separating from a living creeping animal

moves.cueHe: רבי עקיבא אומר: ״שרץ״
moves.summary: derives the creeping-animal exclusion from ״שרץ״: sinews and bones
moves.about: what excludes flesh separating from a living creeping animal — failure to regenerate, or the absence of sinews and bones

moves.cueHe: רבי אומר: ״שרץ״
moves.summary: derives from ״שרץ״ that flesh, sinews and bones are required
moves.about: whether the word שרץ requires only sinews and bones, or flesh, sinews and bones together

moves.cueHe: בין רבי לרבי עקיבא איכא בינייהו ארכובה
moves.summary: states without asking that the leg joint divides Rabbi from R' Akiva here too
moves.about: what practical case separates R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili in the creeping-animal baraita

moves.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי מאי איכא בינייהו?
moves.summary: asks what divides R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili in the creeping-animal baraita
moves.about: what practical case separates R' Yosei HaGelili from R' Akiva in the creeping-animal baraita

moves.cueHe: אמר רב פפא: כוליא וניב שפתים
moves.summary: again the kidney and upper lip
moves.about: the kidney and upper lip of a creeping animal, which have no bone and do not regenerate, divide R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili

moves.cueHe: וצריכא, דאי אשמעינן בהמה
moves.summary: explains why the animal baraita alone would not suffice: a creeping animal, whose impurity operates at a lentil-bulk, might have been treated more stringently
moves.about: why both the animal baraita and the creeping-animal baraita were needed, since neither case alone would have settled the other

moves.cueHe: ואי אשמועינן שרץ
moves.summary: and why the creeping-animal baraita alone would not suffice: an animal, which imparts impurity by carrying, might have been treated more stringently

moves.cueHe: תנו רבנן: החותך כזית בשר מאבר מן החי
moves.summary: opens a new baraita: severing flesh from a limb and only then designating it as food leaves it pure
moves.about: brings the baraita on severing an olive-bulk of flesh from a limb of a living animal and the order of severing and designating it as food

moves.cueHe: חישב עליו, ואחר כך חתכו – טמא
moves.summary: the baraita's second clause: designating first and severing afterwards renders the flesh impure

moves.cueHe: רבי אסי לא על לבי מדרשא
moves.summary: R' Asi, absent from the study hall that day, comes upon R' Zeira
moves.about: R' Asi, having missed the study hall that day, comes upon R' Zeira

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: מאי אמור בבי מדרשא?
moves.summary: asks R' Zeira what was said in the study hall
moves.about: what was said in the study hall that day

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: מאי קשיא לך?
moves.summary: asks in return which matter R' Asi finds difficult
moves.about: which matter R' Asi finds difficult and therefore expects to have been discussed

moves.cueHe: דקתני: חישב ואחר כך חתכו טמא
moves.summary: quotes the baraita's second clause as the source of his difficulty
moves.about: quotes the baraita's second clause — designating the flesh and only then severing it renders it impure — as the difficulty

moves.cueHe: טומאת בית הסתרים היא
moves.summary: the contact between limb and flesh is in a concealed place, and impurity in a concealed place does not render an item impure
moves.about: how the flesh contracts impurity from the limb when the point of contact is a concealed place, and impurity in a concealed place does not render an item impure

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: אף לדידי קשיא לי
moves.summary: relays R' Abba bar Memel's resolution: the baraita follows R' Meir, who holds concealed-place impurity does impart impurity
moves.about: resolving R' Asi's difficulty by relaying R' Abba bar Memel's attribution of the baraita to R' Meir

moves.cueHe: ולאו זימנין סגיאין אמרה קמאי
moves.summary: replies that he has already rejected that answer to R' Abba bar Memel's face, since R' Meir distinguishes impurity that requires hekhsher from impurity that does not
moves.about: whether attributing the baraita to R' Meir helps at all, since R' Meir himself distinguishes impurity that requires the item to be rendered susceptible from impurity that does not

moves.cueHe: אמר רבא: ומאי קושיא? דלמא בשהוכשר
moves.summary: knocks down R' Asi's construal: perhaps the baraita speaks of flesh already rendered susceptible before it was severed
moves.about: whether there is any difficulty at all, since the baraita may be speaking of flesh already rendered susceptible before it was severed

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה רבה בר רב חנן לרבא: למה לי הכשר
moves.summary: asks Rava why hekhsher should be needed at all, since while attached the flesh imparted severe impurity through its parent limb
moves.about: why the flesh should need to be rendered susceptible at all, given that while attached it imparted severe impurity by virtue of its parent limb

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: כששימש, מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: answers that while attached the flesh performed the role of wood, not of food, so it still needs hekhsher — the principle the rest of the sugya applies
moves.about: while attached the flesh served the limb only to constitute it a limb, performing the role of wood rather than of food, so it still needs to be rendered susceptible

moves.cueHe: אמר אביי: הרי אמרו כופת שאור שיחדה לישיבה
moves.summary: brought as the first of several rulings Rava's principle explains: leaven designated for sitting is nullified as food
moves.about: brings the ruling that a mass of hardened leaven designated for sitting is nullified as food

moves.cueHe: טומאתה לאו דאורייתא, דאי סלקא דעתך דאורייתא
moves.summary: infers that its treading-impurity must be rabbinic, since otherwise food would impart severe impurity
moves.about: concluding that the leaven's treading-impurity must be rabbinic, since otherwise we would have found food that imparts severe impurity

moves.cueHe: כששימש – מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: knocks Abaye's inference down with Rava's principle: as a seat the leaven performed the role of wood, so it is impure by Torah law after all
moves.about: rejecting Abaye's explanation that these three impurities must be rabbinic, since in each case the food served a non-food function and so performed the role of wood

moves.cueHe: אמר אביי: הרי אמרו תקרובת עבודה זרה של אוכלין
moves.summary: second case: an idolatrous food offering imparts impurity in a tent
moves.about: brings the ruling that an idolatrous food offering imparts impurity in a tent

moves.cueHe: טומאתה לאו דאורייתא, דאי סלקא דעתך דאורייתא
moves.summary: infers again that the impurity must be rabbinic
moves.about: concluding that the idolatrous offering's impurity must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity

moves.cueHe: כששימש – מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: answers again that as an offering the food performed the role of wood
moves.about: redeploys Rava's principle from 129a.6 — what serves a non-food function served as wood — against each of these explanations

moves.cueHe: אמר אביי: הרי אמרו חבורי אוכלין ככלים דמו
moves.summary: third case: food attached to vessels counts as the vessel
moves.about: brings the ruling that foods attached to vessels are considered like the vessels

moves.cueHe: טומאתן לאו דאורייתא, דאי סלקא דעתך דאורייתא
moves.summary: infers once more that the impurity must be rabbinic
moves.about: concluding that the impurity of food attached to vessels must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity

moves.cueHe: כששימש – מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: answers that in filling the vessel's cracks the food performed the role of wood

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה רב פפא לרבא: הא דתניא, חלב נבלה בכפרים
moves.summary: Rav Pappa puts the same shape of case to Rava: carcass fat in the villages requires designation and hekhsher
moves.about: brings the taught ruling that forbidden fat of a carcass in the villages requires designation as food and rendering-susceptible

moves.cueHe: טומאתו אגב כוליא לאו דאורייתא
moves.summary: infers that the fat's impurity through the kidney must be rabbinic
moves.about: concluding that the fat's impurity by virtue of the kidney must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity

moves.cueHe: כששימש – מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: answers that in shielding the kidney the fat performed the role of wood
moves.about: rejecting Rav Pappa's explanation: the fat's impurity is by Torah law, since in shielding the kidney it performed the role of wood rather than of food

moves.cueHe: אמר רב מתנה: הרי אמרו בית שסככו בזרעים
moves.summary: final case: seeds used to roof a house are rendered pure and become part of the house
moves.about: brings the ruling that seeds used to roof a house are rendered pure, becoming part of the house

moves.cueHe: טומאתו לאו דאורייתא, דאי סלקא דעתך דאורייתא
moves.summary: infers that the impurity of such a house must be rabbinic
moves.about: concluding that the roofed house's impurity must be rabbinic, since seeds cannot impart severe impurity

moves.cueHe: כששימש – מעשה עץ שימש
moves.summary: closes the series: as roofing the seeds performed the role of wood, so the impurity is by Torah law
moves.about: rejecting Rav Mattana's explanation: the seeds impart impurity by Torah law, since as roofing they performed the role of wood rather than of food

edges.cueHe: ״וכי ימות מן הבהמה״ – מקצת בהמה מטמאה
edges.about: reading מן הבהמה as a partitive that excludes a slaughtered tereifa from carcass impurity

edges.cueHe: ״בהמה״, מה בהמה – גידים ועצמות, אף כל – גידים ועצמות

edges.cueHe: ״בהמה״ מה בהמה – בשר גידים ועצמות, אף כל – בשר גידים ועצמות
edges.about: deriving from the word בהמה that only what has flesh, sinews and bones imparts carcass impurity

edges.cueHe: מאי איכא בין רבי לרבי עקיבא?

edges.cueHe: מאי איכא בין רבי לרבי עקיבא?
edges.about: what practical case separates R' Akiva's requirement of sinews and bones from Rabbi's requirement of flesh, sinews and bones
the leg joint, which has sinews and bones but no flesh, is the case that divides them

edges.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי, מאי איכא בינייהו?
edges.about: what practical case separates R' Akiva's sinews-and-bones criterion from R' Yosei HaGelili's non-regeneration criterion

edges.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי, מאי איכא בינייהו?
edges.about: what practical case separates R' Yosei HaGelili's non-regeneration criterion from R' Akiva's sinews-and-bones criterion

edges.cueHe: אמר רב פפא: כוליא וניב שפתים איכא בינייהו
edges.about: the kidney and the upper lip, which do not regenerate but have no bone, are the cases that divide R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili

edges.cueHe: תניא נמי גבי שרצים כהאי גוונא
edges.about: brings the parallel baraita in which the same three tannaim dispute over flesh separating from a living creeping animal
expounding במותם to limit creeping-animal impurity to what does not generate a replacement, excluding flesh
what excludes flesh separating from a living creeping animal — failure to regenerate, or the absence of sinews and bones

edges.about: deriving from the word שרץ that only what has sinews and bones imparts creeping-animal impurity
whether the word שרץ requires only sinews and bones, or flesh, sinews and bones together

edges.cueHe: ״שרץ״, מה שרץ – בשר גידים ועצמות, אף כל – בשר גידים ועצמות
edges.about: deriving from the word שרץ that only what has flesh, sinews and bones imparts creeping-animal impurity

edges.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי מאי איכא בינייהו?
edges.about: what practical case separates R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili in the creeping-animal baraita

edges.cueHe: בין רבי עקיבא לרבי יוסי הגלילי מאי איכא בינייהו?
edges.about: what practical case separates R' Yosei HaGelili from R' Akiva in the creeping-animal baraita

edges.cueHe: אמר רב פפא: כוליא וניב שפתים איכא בינייהו
edges.about: the kidney and upper lip of a creeping animal, which have no bone and do not regenerate, divide R' Akiva from R' Yosei HaGelili
why both the animal baraita and the creeping-animal baraita were needed, since neither case alone would have settled the other
edges.proposedPredicate: interpret.justifies_necessity_of — «וצריכא» — shows why each of two overlapping teachings had to be stated, since either alone would have left room for a contrary inference; interprets says what words mean, supplies_reason_for gives a rule's rationale, and objects_to_redundancy is the opposite move

edges.about: brings the baraita on severing an olive-bulk of flesh from a limb of a living animal and the order of severing and designating it as food
R' Asi, having missed the study hall that day, comes upon R' Zeira

edges.cueHe: אמר ליה: מאי אמור בבי מדרשא?
edges.about: what was said in the study hall that day
which matter R' Asi finds difficult and therefore expects to have been discussed

edges.cueHe: דקתני: חישב ואחר כך חתכו טמא
edges.about: quotes the baraita's second clause — designating the flesh and only then severing it renders it impure — as the difficulty
how the flesh contracts impurity from the limb when the point of contact is a concealed place, and impurity in a concealed place does not render an item impure
R' Zeira reports that he had put this same difficulty to R' Abba bar Memel
R' Zeira relays the answer he received from R' Abba bar Memel
identifying the anonymous baraita with R' Meir, who holds that impurity in a concealed place does render an item impure
adduces R' Meir's ruling that impurity in a concealed place does impart impurity as the ground of the identification

edges.cueHe: אמר ליה: אף לדידי קשיא לי
edges.about: resolving R' Asi's difficulty by relaying R' Abba bar Memel's attribution of the baraita to R' Meir
whether attributing the baraita to R' Meir helps at all, since R' Meir himself distinguishes impurity that requires the item to be rendered susceptible from impurity that does not

edges.cueHe: שני ליה לרבי מאיר בין טומאה דבעיא הכשר ובין טומאה דלא בעיא הכשר
edges.about: claiming that R' Meir concedes concealed-place impurity does not take effect where the item still needs to be rendered susceptible
whether there is any difficulty at all, since the baraita may be speaking of flesh already rendered susceptible before it was severed

edges.cueHe: אמר ליה רבה בר רב חנן לרבא: למה לי הכשר
edges.about: why the flesh should need to be rendered susceptible at all, given that while attached it imparted severe impurity by virtue of its parent limb
while attached the flesh served the limb only to constitute it a limb, performing the role of wood rather than of food, so it still needs to be rendered susceptible

edges.cueHe: הרי אמרו כופת שאור שיחדה לישיבה – בטלה
edges.about: brings the ruling that a mass of hardened leaven designated for sitting is nullified as food
concluding that the leaven's treading-impurity must be rabbinic, since otherwise we would have found food that imparts severe impurity

edges.cueHe: הרי אמרו תקרובת עבודה זרה של אוכלין מטמאין באוהל
edges.about: brings the ruling that an idolatrous food offering imparts impurity in a tent
concluding that the idolatrous offering's impurity must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity

edges.cueHe: הרי אמרו חבורי אוכלין ככלים דמו
edges.about: brings the ruling that foods attached to vessels are considered like the vessels
concluding that the impurity of food attached to vessels must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity
rejecting Abaye's explanation that these three impurities must be rabbinic, since in each case the food served a non-food function and so performed the role of wood
redeploys Rava's principle from 129a.6 — what serves a non-food function served as wood — against each of these explanations

edges.cueHe: הא דתניא, חלב נבלה בכפרים צריך מחשבה והכשר
edges.about: brings the taught ruling that forbidden fat of a carcass in the villages requires designation as food and rendering-susceptible
concluding that the fat's impurity by virtue of the kidney must be rabbinic, since food cannot impart severe impurity
whether Rava's 'served as wood' principle can stand, given the taught ruling on carcass fat in the villages which Rav Pappa explains as only rabbinically impure
rejecting Rav Pappa's explanation: the fat's impurity is by Torah law, since in shielding the kidney it performed the role of wood rather than of food

edges.cueHe: הרי אמרו בית שסככו בזרעים – טהרו
edges.about: brings the ruling that seeds used to roof a house are rendered pure, becoming part of the house
concluding that the roofed house's impurity must be rabbinic, since seeds cannot impart severe impurity
rejecting Rav Mattana's explanation: the seeds impart impurity by Torah law, since as roofing they performed the role of wood rather than of food

adduces Rav's other derivation from the same verse — some animals impart carcass impurity and some do not — as the material of the difficulty
brings the baraita on flesh separating from a living animal, with the derivations of R' Yosei HaGelili, R' Akiva and Rabbi
R' Zeira relays the answer he received from R' Abba bar Memel
adduces R' Meir's ruling that impurity in a concealed place does impart impurity as the ground of the identification
